roundShape.why: All three are test files: my own red test, the real-stack harness it pins, and the hold test I handed the implementer. No product file changed since f41a4d8c, so round 11's live runs, its controls and its race run stand for the code that merges, and this round proves what this round changed.

implementerProof.how: I drove both of this round's claims myself rather than reading them: my red test is green here with its body unchanged and red against the old freePort, and the hold test the implementer committed is byte-for-byte the one I handed over and passes twenty times running. I also measured the fix's limit, below, which the implementer's proof does not state.

proof.criterion: Round 11's red test is answered: the real-stack harness chooses its ports so that one port cannot be handed to two processes of one stack
proof.surface: The harness's own exported chooser, driven by the test I wrote in round 11, in this pod
proof.observed: 2 pass, 0 fail, 4,000 expect() calls — the 2,000 rounds of the distinctness case and the bind-back case. My test's body is unchanged: the whole diff from my commit d8eecf87 to this head is the two import lines swapped for biome's order, nothing else. `freePorts(count)` (envoy-stack.ts:71) holds every probe socket open until all count ports are chosen and closes them in a `finally`, and `startEnvoyStack` takes its three in one call.
proof.negativeControl: Two, both reverted. (1) The harness restored to f41a4d8c's one-at-a-time `freePort`: the test fails at once, `SyntaxError: Export named 'freePorts' not found`, 1 fail — the seam the fix adds is what the test asks for. (2) The sharper one, the old algorithm behind the new seam (freePorts rewritten to probe and close one port at a time): 2 pass, three runs in a row. That is the honest limit of my own test and I state it rather than let it read as a lock — see `testLimit` below.

proof.criterion: A relay holding a message another path is pushing delays only that session, and pushes the held message once the attempt record clears
proof.surface: The listener package's real stack (natsd, the listener's own relays, two serving-port sessions), the test I wrote in round 11 and handed over, as the implementer committed it
proof.observed: ok github.com/sjawhar/envoy/cmd/listener 62.141s — twenty runs, no failure. The committed file is the one I handed over: same assertions, same bounds (the hold's log line within 30 s, the other session's message at its port within 20 s, the held session pushed nothing at that moment, the held message within 30 s of the clear and not a second time within 2 s).
proof.negativeControl: Measured in round 11 on the identical body and still standing, since no product file changed since: one package-level mutex around holdWhilePushedElsewhere in pushUntilAccepted (so every session's judgement serializes) → FAIL, 'the other session's message … never reached its port while ses_held_… held one'; and the attempt record never cleared → FAIL, 'the held message … never reached the port after the other push ended'.

testLimit: My free-ports distinctness case is a guaranteed pass for the correct chooser and only a probabilistic detector of a revert, and I would rather say so than have a later reader trust it further than it goes. In round 11 I measured the old algorithm repeating a port in 1 triple of 2,000 — taken while two live e2e runs were churning this pod's ports. On an idle pod I now measure 0 duplicates in 20,000 triples, and 0 in 3,000 under a churn loop of my own, so that 1-in-2,000 is not reproducible on demand and the case would catch a revert only sometimes. The bind-back case is deterministic and does lock the fix against a version that keeps its probe sockets open.
residualRisk: The fix removes one of the two ways that error can happen, and I could not attribute CI's failure to the one it removes. `freePorts` closes every probe before `startEnvoyStack` starts natsd and the listener, so a process outside this test still has a window to take one of the three ports between the close and the children's binds; what the fix makes impossible is the stack handing one port to two of its own processes. The listener's log line at job 124443217959 names only the port it could not bind, not who held it, so I cannot say which of the two reddened that run. If envoy-session-stall fails this way again, the remedy that covers both is for startEnvoyStack to retry on a child's EADDRINUSE rather than to choose better; it is not worth doing before a second occurrence, and it is the architect's to schedule.
